claim: Plasma Membrane is the primary structure for adjusting to ever changing conditions.
source: Plasma Membrane is the primary structure for adjusting to ever changing conditions.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract without specific experimental data or citations provided in this sentence.

claim: PM sub-compartmentalization in domains is thought to orchestrate signaling.
source: PM sub-compartmentalization in domains is thought to orchestrate signaling.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific understanding about membrane organization.

claim: REMORINs are plant-specific proteins regulating hormonal crosstalk and host invasion.
source: The plant-specific REMORINs are proteins regulating hormonal crosstalk and host invasion.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by the broader literature context.

claim: REMs are the best-characterized nanodomain markers.
source: REMs are the best-characterized nanodomain markers via an uncharacterized moiety called REMORIN C-terminal Anchor.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Targeting of REMORIN is independent of the COP-II-dependent secretory pathway.
source: We showed that targeting of REMORINis independent of the COP-II-dependent secretory pathway and mediated by PI4P and sterol.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and related experiments.

claim: Targeting of REMORIN is mediated by PI4P and sterol.
source: We showed that targeting of REMORINis independent of the COP-II-dependent secretory pathway and mediated by PI4P and sterol.
evidence: This is supported by experimental manipulations shown in Figure 1C and 1E.

claim: REM-CA is an unconventional lipid-binding motif that confers nanodomain organization.
source: REM-CA is an unconventional lipid-binding motif that confers nanodomain organization.
evidence: This is supported by biophysical and structural data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Mobility and supramolecular organization are critical for immunity.
source: Analyzes of REM-CA mutants by single particle tracking demonstrate that mobility and supramolecular organization are critical for immunity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the functional assays with REM-CA mutants shown in Figures 4-6.

claim: Membrane compartmentalization is critical for cell signaling and therefore for development and survival of organisms.
source: Emerging evidences suggest that membrane compartmentalization is critical for cell signaling and therefore for development and survival of organisms ( Grecco et al., 2011 ).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Grecco et al., 2011.

claim: REMs belong to a multigenic family of six groups encoding plant-specific membrane-bound proteins involved in responses to biotic and abiotic stimuli.
source: REMs belong to a multigenic family of six groups encoding plant-specific membrane-bound proteins involved in responses to biotic and abiotic stimuli ( Raffaele et al., 2009 ; Jarsch et al., 2014 ; Jarsch and Ott, 2011 ; Raffaele et al., 2007 ; Gui et al., 2014 ; Jamann et al., 2016 ).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: In Solanaceae, group 1 REMs limit the spreading of Potato Virus X (PVX), without affecting viral replication.
source: in Solanaceae , group 1 REMs limit the spreading of Potato Virus X ( PVX ), without affecting viral replication ( Raffaele et al., 2009 )
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Raffaele et al., 2009.

claim: Group 1 REMs promote susceptibility to Phytophthora infestans.
source: and promote susceptibility to Phytophthora infestans ( Bozkurt et al., 2014 ).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bozkurt et al., 2014.

claim: A group 2 REM was described as essential during nodulation process in Medicago truncatula.
source: A group 2 REM was described as essential during nodulation process in Medicago truncatula ( Lefebvre et al., 2010 ; Tóth et al., 2012 ).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lefebvre et al., 2010 and Tóth et al., 2012.

claim: In rice, a group 4 REM is upregulated by abscissic acid and negatively regulates brassinosteroid signaling output.
source: In rice, a group 4 REM is upregulated by abscissic acid and negatively regulates brassinosteroid signaling output ( Gui et al., 2016 ).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gui et al., 2016.

claim: Arabidopsis group 4 REMs play a role as positive regulators of geminiviral infection.
source: Arabidopsis group 4 REMs also play a role as positive regulators of geminiviral infection ( Son et al., 2014 ).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Son et al., 2014.

claim: Group 1 and group 6 REMs regulate the PM-lined cytoplasmic channels called plasmodesmata (PD).
source: Finally, group 1 and group 6 REMs regulate the PM-lined cytoplasmic channels called plasmodesmata ( PD ), specialized nanochannels allowing intercellular communication in plants.
evidence: This is supported by the context and citations that follow.

claim: Group 1 and group 6 REM isoforms were found to be able to modify PD aperture leading to a modification of viral movement.
source: Remarkably, these latter isoforms of REMs were found to be able to modify PD aperture leading to a modification of viral movement ( Raffaele et al., 2009 ; Perraki et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Raffaele et al., 2009 and Perraki et al., 2014.

claim: Group 6 REMs have an impact on the grain setting in rice.
source: and an impact on the grain setting in rice, respectively ( Gui et al., 2014 ).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gui et al., 2014.

claim: REMs need to localize to the PM to fulfill their functions.
source: To fulfill these functions, REMs need to localize to the PM ( Perraki et al., 2012 ; Bozkurt et al., 2014 ).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Perraki et al., 2012 and Bozkurt et al., 2014.

claim: REM-CA is a novel membrane-binding domain shaped by convergent evolution among unrelated putative PM-binding domains in bacterial, viral and animal proteins.
source: Our groups defined a short peptide located at the C-terminal domain of REM, called REM-CA (REM C-terminal Anchor) as a novel membrane-binding domain shaped by convergent evolution among unrelated putative PM-binding domains in bacterial, viral and animal proteins. ( Perraki et al., 2012 ; Raffaele et al., 2013 ; Konrad et al., 2014 ).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Perraki et al., 2012, Raffaele et al., 2013, and Konrad et al., 2014.

claim: REM-CA is necessary for PM localization of REMs.
source: REM-CA is necessary for PM localization of REMs and sufficient to target a given soluble protein ( eg GFP) to the PM
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited in the introduction.

claim: REM-CA is sufficient to target a given soluble protein (eg GFP) to the PM.
source: REM-CA is necessary for PM localization of REMs and sufficient to target a given soluble protein ( eg GFP) to the PM
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited in the introduction.

claim: REM-CA binds in vitro to poly phosphoinositides.
source: REM-CA binds in vitro to poly phosphoinositidesbut the association of REM-CA with the PM is not limited to electrostatic interactions
evidence: This is supported by citation to Perraki et al., 2012.

claim: The association of REM-CA with the PM is not limited to electrostatic interactions.
source: REM-CA binds in vitro to poly phosphoinositidesbut the association of REM-CA with the PM is not limited to electrostatic interactions and the final interaction with PM display anchor properties similar to intrinsic protein ( Perraki et al., 2012 ).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Perraki et al., 2012.

claim: The final interaction of REM-CA with PM displays anchor properties similar to intrinsic protein.
source: and the final interaction with PM display anchor properties similar to intrinsic protein ( Perraki et al., 2012 ).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Perraki et al., 2012.

claim: REM-CA can be S-acylated.
source: REM-CA can be S-acylated ( Hemsley et al., 2013 )
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hemsley et al., 2013.

claim: S-acylation is not the determinant for REM localization to membrane domains.
source: although this modification is not the determinant for their localization to membrane domains, since deacylated versions of some REMs remain able to localize to membrane domains ( Jarsch and Ott, 2011 ; Hemsley et al., 2013 ).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jarsch and Ott, 2011 and Hemsley et al., 2013.

claim: Deacylated versions of some REMs remain able to localize to membrane domains.
source: since deacylated versions of some REMs remain able to localize to membrane domains ( Jarsch and Ott, 2011 ; Hemsley et al., 2013 ).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jarsch and Ott, 2011 and Hemsley et al., 2013.

claim: St REM1.3 is a trimeric protein.
source: St REM1.3 is a trimeric protein ( Perraki et al., 2012 )
evidence: This is supported by citation to Perraki et al., 2012.

claim: St REM1.3 strictly localizes to the PM.
source: St REM1.3 is a trimeric protein ( Perraki et al., 2012 ) that strictly localizes to the PM
evidence: This is supported by citation to Perraki et al., 2012.

claim: St REM1.3 segregates in a sterol-dependent manner into ca. 100 nm nanodomains.
source: and segregates in a sterol-dependent manner into ca. 100 nm nanodomains ( Raffaele et al., 2009 ; Demir et al., 2013 ).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Raffaele et al., 2009 and Demir et al., 2013.

claim: St REM1.3 is a functional homolog of the PM-localized Nicotinana benthamiana endogenous group 1b REMs toward the restriction of Potato Virus X (PVX) spreading.
source: In this context, we showed that St REM1.3 is a functional homolog of the PM-localized Nicotinana benthamiana endogenous group 1b REMs toward the restriction of Potato Virus X ( PVX ) spreading.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nb REM1.2 and Nb REM1.3 isoforms are highly expressed in leaf epidermis.
source: Consistently, Nb REM1.2 and Nb REM1.3 isoforms are highly expressed in leaf epidermis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: PVX is a mechanically transmitted virus for which the infection initiates in the epidermis and spreads from cell-to-cell via different tissues to reach the phloem vasculature and infect the whole plant.
source: Importantly, PVX is a mechanically transmitted virus for which the infection initiates in the epidermis and spreads from cell-to-cell via different tissues to reach the phloem vasculature and infect the whole plant ( Cruz et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cruz et al., 1998.

claim: YFP-St REM1.3 was normally targeted to the PM upon inhibition of COP-II-mediated ER-to-Golgi trafficking by overexpression of a dominant-negative SAR1.
source: Consistent to what was shown for the rice group 4 REM ( Gui et al., 2015 ), YFP- St REM1.3 was normally targeted to the PM upon inhibition of COP-II-mediated ER-to-Golgi trafficking by overexpression of a dominant-negative SAR1 ( de Marcos Lousa et al., 2016 )
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citations.

claim: YFP-St REM1.3 was normally targeted to the PM upon treatment with Brefeldin A (BFA).
source: or by treatment with Brefeldin A ( BFA), a pharmacological inhibitor of ADP-ribosylation factor 1-GTPase and its effectors, ARF-guanine-exchange factors, of the COP-I-mediated secretory pathway ( Peyroche et al., 1999 ) ( Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3 ).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3, and citation to Peyroche et al., 1999.

claim: Organization of YFP-St REM1.3 in the plane of the PM was not affected in the presence of dominant-negative SAR1.
source: Moreover, organization of YFP- St REM1.3 in the plane of the PM was not affected in the presence of dominant-negative SAR1 ( Figure 1B )
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Fenpropimorph (fen) alters the PM sterol-composition but not the total amount of sterols.
source: Fen alters the PM sterol-composition but not the total amount of sterols (Grison et al., 2015; Hartmann et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grison et al., 2015 and Hartmann et al., 2002.

claim: After fen treatment, the content of ∆5-sterols decreased concurrently with an increase in cycloartenol.
source: As expected, after fen treatment, the content of ∆5-sterols decreased concurrently with an increase in cycloartenol (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Qualitative modification of sterol composition had no effect on the targeting of YFP-StREM1.3 to the PM but abolished its nanodomain organization.
source: This qualitative modification of sterol composition had no effect on the targeting of YFP-StREM1.3 to the PM but abolished its nanodomain organization measured by the SCI (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Nanodomains enriched in YFP-StREM1.3 co-localized with highly ordered regions of the PM.
source: Figure 1D shows that nanodomains enriched in YFP-StREM1.3 co-localized with highly ordered regions of the PM
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: PI4P is enriched in the inner-leaflet of plant PM, conferring a negatively charged electrostatic field that defines PM identity in regard to other endomembranes.
source: Recent works showed that PI4P is enriched in the inner-leaflet of plant PM, conferring a negatively charged electrostatic field that defines PM identity in regard to other endomembranes ( Vermeer et al., 2009 ; Simon et al., 2016 , Simon et al., 2014 ).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vermeer et al., 2009, Simon et al., 2016, and Simon et al., 2014.

claim: MAP-mTU2-SAC1p specifically dephosphorylates PI4P at the PM level.
source: To alter the PI4P content, we used the Myristoylated / Palmitoylated-Phosphatidylinositol 4-phoshatase SAC1p enzyme from yeast ( Hammond et al., 2012 ) fused to mTurquoise2 (MAP-mTU2-SAC1p) which specifically dephosphorylates PI4P at the PM level ( Hammond et al., 2012Hammond et al., 2012 ) Hammond et al., 2012 ; Stefan et al., 2011; Mesmin et al., 2013 ; Moser von Filseck et al., 2015a , Moser von Filseck et al., 2015b )
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hammond et al., 2012, Stefan et al., 2011, Mesmin et al., 2013, Moser von Filseck et al., 2015a, and Moser von Filseck et al., 2015b.

claim: MAP-SAC1p does not impact PS or PI(4,5)P2.
source: without impacting PS or PI (4,5) P 2 ( Simon et al., 2016 ) ( Figure 1—figure supplement 6 ).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Simon et al., 2016 and experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Expression of the active form of MAP-SAC1p induced a reduction in PM-associated PI4P concentration leading to a strong decrease of both YFP-St REM1.3 signal and lateral segregation at the PM.
source: Compared to the expression of the dead version of MAP-SAC1p, the expression of the active form induced a reduction in PM-associated PI4P concentration leading to a strong decrease of both YFP- St REM1.3 signal and lateral segregation at the PM ( Figure 1E ).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: PI4P is required for the targeting of St REM1.3 at the PM and for its sub-compartmentalization within the PM plane.
source: These data suggest that PI4P is required for the targeting of St REM1.3 at the PM and for its sub-compartmentalization within the PM plane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data with MAP-SAC1p shown in Figure 1E.

claim: REM-CA peptide is unstructured in aqueous environment.
source: First, liquid-state NMR spectra of REM-CA in aqueous environment showed that REM-CA peptide is unstructured ( Perraki et al., 2012 ) ( Figure 2—Figure supplement 1A ).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Perraki et al., 2012 and experimental data shown in Figure 2—Figure supplement 1A.

claim: REM-CA folds into an alpha helical conformation in hydrophobic environment.
source: Second, equivalent spectra, acquired in hydrophobic environment showed that REM-CA folds into an alpha helical conformation ( Figure 2—Figure supplement 1A ).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—Figure supplement 1A.

claim: REM-CA's partial insertion into liposomes increased the degree of order of the first 10 carbon atoms of acyl chains.
source: In these conditions, REM-CA's partial insertion into liposomes increased the degree of order of the first 10 carbon atoms of acyl chains indicated that REM-CA is partially embedded in the lipid phase ( Figure 2B ).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: REM-CA insertion does not modify the overall bilayer structure.
source: Importantly, REM-CA insertion does not modify the overall bilayer structure as suggested by a very similar global thermotropism ( Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E ).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: In silico analyzes predicted that REM-CA is structurally divided into two regions: a putative helical region (171-190aa, called Region 1, R1) and a more hydrophobic non-helical region (191-198aa called Region 2, R2).
source: In silico analyzes predicted that REM-CA is structurally divided into two regions ( Figure 2—figure supplement 2 ): a putative helical region (171-190aa, called Region 1, R1) and a more hydrophobic non-helical region (191-198aa called Region 2, R2).
evidence: This is supported by in silico analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The penetration capacity of the peptide REM-CA was higher in the monolayers composed of PC, PIPs and sitosterols, than in monolayers composed of PC alone.
source: Adsorption assays showed that the penetration capacity of the peptide REM-CA was higher in the monolayers composed of PC, PIPs and sitosterols, than in monolayers composed of PC alone ( Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Peptide R2 but not the R1 was able to insert into monolayers.
source: Furthermore, peptide R2 but not the R1 was able to insert into monolayers ( Figure 2C ).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Deletion of R2 in the REM-CA of YFP-St REM1.3 abolished PM association in planta.
source: Consistently, deletion of R2 in the REM-CA of YFP- St REM1.3 abolished PM association in planta ( Figure 2D ).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: FT-IR showed a maximum intensity shift in the absorbance wavenumber of lipid phosphate groups in the presence of REM-CA, R1 and R2 peptides, with a stronger effect of R1 as compared to R2.
source: FT-IR showed a maximum intensity shift in the absorbance wavenumber of lipid phosphate groups in the presence of REM-CA, R1 and R2 peptides, with a stronger effect of R1 as compared to R2 ( Figure 2—figure supplement 3B ).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The polar heads of lipids are involved in the REM-CA-liposome interactions.
source: This clearly shows that the polar heads of lipids are involved in the REM-CA-liposome interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FT-IR data.

claim: A maximum intensity shift in the absorbance wavenumber of carbon-hydrogen bonds was observed in presence of R2.
source: Moreover, a maximum intensity shift in the absorbance wavenumber of carbon-hydrogen bonds was observed in presence of R2, which confirmed that R2 is more embedded than R1 within the lipid phase ( Figure 2E ).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: R2 is more embedded than R1 within the lipid phase.
source: which confirmed that R2 is more embedded than R1 within the lipid phase ( Figure 2E ).
evidence: This is an inference based on the FT-IR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: REM-CA, R1 and R2 peptides are mainly a mix of different structures in PC-containing liposomes.
source: FT-IR experiments showed that REM-CA, R1 and R2 peptides are mainly a mix of different structures in PC-containing liposomes (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: R1 was more helical and R2 was more extended when sitosterol and PIPs are present in the bilayer.
source: In contrast, R1 was more helical and R2 was more extended when sitosterol and PIPs are present in the bilayer (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: PIPs were sufficient to induce R1, R2 and REM-CA folding.
source: Importantly, PIPs were sufficient to induce R1, R2 and REM-CA folding (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Solid-state NMR spectra confirmed that R1 adopted a single non-helical conformation in PC, while partially folding into an alpha helix in the presence of PIPs and sitosterol.
source: Solid-state NMR spectra confirmed that R1 adopted a single non-helical conformation in PC, while partially folding into an alpha helix in the presence of PIPs and sitosterol (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: MD confirmed that REM-CA inserted itself in the lipid bilayer and presented two distinct regions.
source: MD confirmed that REM-CA inserted itself in the lipid bilayer and presented two distinct regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A)
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The lateral ring of tyrosine Y184 was unlikely to interact with sterols with a distance between Y184 and sterol superior to 1 µm.
source: MD proposed that albeit facing the inside of the bilayer (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), the lateral ring of tyrosine Y184 (tyrosine being a residue often observed in interaction with sterols [Nasir and Besson, 2011]) was unlikely to interact with sterols with a distance between Y184 and sterol superior to 1 µm (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Lysines and arginine present in REM-CA, namely K192 and K193, and to a lesser extent K183 and R185, can form salt-bridges with the phosphate groups of PI4P.
source: MD also modeled that lysines and arginine present in REM-CA, namely K192 and K193, and to a lesser extent K183 and R185, can form salt-bridges with the phosphate groups of PI4P (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The lysine K176 was not in interaction with PI4P.
source: The lysine K176 was not in interaction with PI4P.
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data.

claim: The YFP-StREM1.3 Y184F mutant was still organized in PM nanodomains.
source: Consistent with a lack of interaction with sterols (Figure 2H), the YFP-StREM1.3 Y184F mutant was still organized in PM nanodomains (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Single and double mutants of the four lysines and the arginine present in REM-CA still localized to the PM.
source: Confocal microscopy images presented in Figure 3C show that single and double mutants still localized to the PM.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A strong impairment in PM-targeting with full or partial localization in the cytosol was observed for all triple to sextuple mutants of the four lysines and the arginine present in REM-CA.
source: In contrast, a strong impairment in PM-targeting with full or partial localization in the cytosol was observed for all triple to sextuple mutants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The net electrostatic charge of REM-CA mutants is negative.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to membrane surface-charge targeted proteins which generally possess a net charge of up to +8 (Simon et al., 2016; Heo et al., 2006; Yeung et al., 2008; Barbosa et al., 2014), the net electrostatic charge of REM-CA mutants is negative (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and citations.

claim: The REM-CA/PM coupling is controlled by a specific lipid-peptide interaction, primarily governed by the intrinsic structural properties of the REM-CA moiety, and not by its net charge.
source: This suggests that the REM-CA/PM coupling is controlled by a specific lipid-peptide interaction, primarily governed by the intrinsic structural properties of the REM-CA moiety, and not by its net charge.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that REM-CA mutants have negative net charge but still localize to PM.

claim: Mutating K192, K193, and K183 revealed the requirement of these residues for a correct nanodomain organization.
source: Consistently with MD calculations of the distance with the PI4P polar-head (Figure 2H), mutating K192, K193, and K183 revealed the requirement of these residues for a correct nanodomain organization
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B and MD calculations in Figure 2H.

claim: K176 and R185 taken alone are dispensable for nanodomain organization.
source: whereas K176 and R185 taken alone are dispensable.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The coupling of K183, K192 and K193 mutations with other mutations on charged residues increased the alteration of StREM1.3 PM-nanodomain organization.
source: Moreover, the coupling of K183, K192 and K193 mutations with other mutations on charged residues increased the alteration of StREM1.3 PM-nanodomain organization as assessed by the SCI (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Single mutants K176S, Y184F and R185A behaved like St REM1.3 WT in restricting cell-to-cell propagation of PVX.
source: Single mutants K176S, Y184F and R185A behaved like St REM1.3 WT
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, D.

claim: K183S, K192A and K193A partially lost their ability to reduce viral intercellular movement and PD permeability.
source: whereas K183S and K192A and K193A partially lost their ability to reduce viral intercellular movement and PD permeability ( Figure 4C, D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: REM-CA double mutants showed a close to complete loss of activity in reducing viral intercellular movement and PD permeability.
source: A close to complete loss of activity was observed with REM-CA double mutants
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, D.

claim: All EOS-St REM1.3 fusions exhibited a typically highly confined diffusion mode.
source: All EOS- St REM1.3 fusions exhibited a typically highly confined diffusion mode
evidence: This is supported by spt-PALM data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The four EOS-StREM1.3 mutants show a lower mobility than the EOS-StREM1.3 WT.
source: but the four EOS-StREM1.3 mutants show a lower mobility than the EOS-StREM1.3 WT ( Figure 5B, C ).
evidence: This is supported by spt-PALM data shown in Figure 5B, C.

claim: EOS-St REM1.3 K183S displayed a similar MSD than EOS-St REM1.3 WT.
source: Nevertheless, EOS- St REM1.3 K183S displayed a similar MSD than EOS- St REM1.3 WTwhereas EOS- St REM1.3 K192A , EOS- St REM1.3 K183S / K192A and EOS- St REM1.3 K192A / K193A displayed a lower MSD ( Figure 5D ).
evidence: This is supported by spt-PALM data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: EOS-St REM1.3 K192A, EOS-St REM1.3 K183S/K192A and EOS-St REM1.3 K192A/K193A displayed a lower MSD than EOS-St REM1.3 WT.
source: whereas EOS- St REM1.3 K192A , EOS- St REM1.3 K183S / K192A and EOS- St REM1.3 K192A / K193A displayed a lower MSD ( Figure 5D ).
evidence: This is supported by spt-PALM data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: EOS-StREM1.3 WT clustered in nanodomains with a mean diameter of ca. 80 nm.
source: EOS-StREM1.3 WT clustered in nanodomains with a mean diameter of ca. 80 nm, a result in good agreement with previous studies using different methods of imagery (Raffaele et al., 2009; Demir et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by live PALM data and citations to Raffaele et al., 2009 and Demir et al., 2013.

claim: For the WT protein fusion, nanodomains represented ca. 7% of the total PM surface.
source: For the WT protein fusion, nanodomains represented ca. 7% of the total PM surface (Figure 6C)
evidence: This is supported by live PALM data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: For the WT protein fusion, ca. 37% of molecules are in nanodomains.
source: with ca. 37% of molecules in nanodomains (Figure 6D)
evidence: This is supported by live PALM data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: For the WT protein fusion, there is a density of ca. two nanodomains per µm.
source: and a density of ca. two nanodomains per µm (Raffaele et al., 2009) (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by live PALM data shown in Figure 6E and citation to Raffaele et al., 2009.

claim: The four REM-CA mutants showed a decrease of the total surface occupied by nanodomains in the total PM surface.
source: Interestingly, the four REM-CA mutants showed a decrease of the total surface occupied by nanodomains in the total PM surface (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by live PALM data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: EOS-StREM1.3K183S and StREM1.3K183S/K192A display smaller nanodomains with a lower number of molecules per cluster.
source: EOS-StREM1.3K183S and StREM1.3K183S/K192A display smaller nanodomains with a lower number of molecules per cluster
evidence: This is supported by live PALM data shown in Figure 6.

claim: EOS-StREM1.3K192A, and EOS-StREM1.3K192A/K193A displayed larger nanodomains with a decrease of overall nanodomain density in the PM.
source: whereas EOS-StREM1.3K192A, and EOS-StREM1.3K192A/K193A displayed larger nanodomains with a decrease of overall nanodomain density in the PM (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is supported by live PALM data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Single protein mobility behavior and protein supramolecular organization are uncoupled.
source: The study of REM-CA mutants revealed that single protein mobility behavior and protein supramolecular organization are uncoupled
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutants with different mobility show different organization patterns.

claim: EOS-StREM1.3K192A proteins display the lower MSD but form larger clusters.
source: for example EOS-StREM1.3K192A proteins displaying the lower MSD but forms larger clusters.
evidence: This is supported by spt-PALM and live PALM data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Mutations in REM-CA affect the mobility and the organization of the protein by altering the partition of St REM1.3 molecules into nanodomains.
source: Altogether, spt-PALM and live PALM data analyzes showed that mutations in REM-CA affect the mobility and the organization of the protein by altering the partition of St REM1.3 molecules into nanodomains ( Figures 3–6 )
